questions.stem: An OT student has 90 items left and 60 minutes remaining on a computer-based certification exam. What is the MOST effective next step?
options: Answer every remaining item with detailed re-reading of each stem
Mark a consistent answer choice for all remaining items, then revisit as time allows
Leave the remaining items blank to avoid penalty
Restart the exam tutorial to reduce anxiety
rationales: Too slow given the time remaining.
Correct — guessing carries no penalty and preserves review time.
Blank answers score zero; unanswered items waste the guessing odds.
The tutorial cannot be reopened and would consume exam time.
questions.reasoning_principle: When time is limited, protect your ability to attempt every item before polishing any single one — an unanswered item always scores zero, a guess never does.
questions.textbook_pointer: Review the time-management strategies in Chapter 1 of your TherapyEd book.

questions.stem: A client recovering from a distal radius fracture is fitted with a wrist cock-up splint and reports the splint feels tight across the palm and limits finger movement. What should the OT do FIRST?
options: Trim the splint's palmar edge back to just proximal to the distal palmar crease
Tell the client to wear the splint fewer hours per day
Tighten the strap closest to the wrist
Refer the client to a hand surgeon before making any changes
rationales: Correct — a trim line crossing the distal palmar crease blocks MCP flexion; trimming it back restores finger movement while keeping wrist support.
Wear schedule affects skin tolerance, not a fit problem that is blocking motion right now.
A tighter proximal strap would not change how far the palmar edge extends.
This is a routine fit adjustment within OT scope — it doesn't need a surgical referral first.
questions.reasoning_principle: Fix the specific design feature causing the functional limitation before changing wear time or escalating to another provider.
questions.textbook_pointer: Review splint trim-line landmarks in the orthotics section of Chapter 3.

questions.stem: An OT is evaluating a new client and has limited time before the first treatment session. What information is MOST important to gather during this initial evaluation?
options: A brief informal impression of the client's mood that day
Standardized, normed measures of the client's current occupational performance
A full family history going back multiple generations
The client's opinion of their previous therapist
rationales: Mood can be noted, but it isn't the priority baseline data the plan of care depends on.
Correct — standardized, normed measures give a comparable baseline to guide goals and track progress.
Extended family history is rarely relevant to establishing an occupational therapy baseline.
This doesn't inform the current client's functional baseline.
questions.reasoning_principle: When evaluation time is limited, prioritize the data that will anchor goal-setting and let you measure change later — not incidental details.
questions.textbook_pointer: Review the purpose of standardized vs. non-standardized assessment in Chapter 5.

questions.stem: A client with a recent hip replacement is preparing for discharge home alone in three days. What should the OT do NEXT?
options: Coordinate a home safety evaluation before the discharge date
Instruct the client to resume driving immediately after discharge
Tell the client to avoid all household tasks indefinitely
Discontinue therapy once the client can walk with a walker
rationales: Correct — a home safety evaluation identifies hazards while there's still time to address them before discharge.
Driving clearance typically requires physician sign-off, not immediate resumption.
Avoiding all tasks indefinitely undermines independence and is not standard guidance.
Walking with a walker doesn't confirm ADL safety at home; discharge readiness needs broader evidence.
questions.reasoning_principle: With a fixed discharge date approaching, act on the step that closes the biggest safety gap while there is still time to fix it.
questions.textbook_pointer: Review discharge planning and home safety recommendations in Chapter 2.

questions.stem: During a session, a client says their hand "feels weak today," and the OT measures grip strength at 5 lbs below the client's baseline. Which detail should the OT document in the Subjective section of the SOAP note?
options: The client's own statement that their hand feels weak today
The 5-lb grip strength measurement
The OT's interpretation of why strength dropped
The plan for next session's grip strengthening activities
rationales: Correct — Subjective captures the client's own words and reported experience.
A measured value belongs in Objective, not Subjective.
Clinical interpretation belongs in Assessment, not Subjective.
Next steps belong in Plan, not Subjective.
questions.reasoning_principle: Sort each detail by its source: what the client says is Subjective, what you measure or observe is Objective — mixing them up weakens the clinical record.
questions.textbook_pointer: Review SOAP note structure and terminology in Chapter 4.

questions.stem: A client with left-sided hemiparesis after a stroke is beginning independent dressing practice and struggles to get their affected arm through a sleeve. What is the MOST appropriate next action?
options: Have the client practice dressing the affected arm first, every time, before the unaffected side
Have a caregiver fully dress the client to avoid frustration
Introduce a button hook and other adaptive equipment right away
Pause dressing practice until the client's strength has fully returned
rationales: Correct — dressing the affected limb first prevents it from being trapped in the garment and builds the habit early.
Full caregiver dressing removes the practice opportunity the client needs to regain independence.
Adaptive equipment is added only once standard technique proves insufficient, not as the first move.
Waiting for full strength return delays functional practice and independence unnecessarily.
questions.reasoning_principle: Start with the least restrictive approach that still builds the skill directly, and add equipment or assistance only once that proves insufficient.
questions.textbook_pointer: Review hemiparesis dressing retraining techniques in Chapter 6.

coach_feedback.scaffold_hint: Look again at what happens to an item you leave blank versus one where you guess — does the exam actually treat those two the same way? Take another look at the case with that in mind, and pick again.
coach_feedback.feedback: Your reasoning connects the time constraint to a concrete decision, which is exactly the kind of judgment this section rewards. Naming that guessing carries no penalty, and using that to protect review time, shows you understand the strategy — not just the rule.
coach_feedback.next_step: Now think about a client whose pacing struggles come from test anxiety rather than a skill gap — what is the underlying cause you'd need to identify before choosing a coaching strategy for them?
coach_feedback.textbook_pointer: See the test-taking strategy tables in Chapter 1 of your TherapyEd book.

coach_feedback.scaffold_hint: Re-read exactly where the client says the tightness is — the palm, not the wrist itself. Which part of the splint's shape sits directly over that spot? Take another look at the case with that in mind, and pick again.
coach_feedback.feedback: You correctly linked the tight, restrictive feeling to the splint's fit rather than to wear time or exercise. That's the right level of reasoning — tracing a symptom back to a specific design feature instead of a general habit.
coach_feedback.trap: overreading the stem and adding facts that are not there
coach_feedback.next_step: How would you adjust the splint pattern itself so it still supports the wrist without crossing the palmar crease?
coach_feedback.textbook_pointer: Review splint trim-line landmarks in the orthotics section of Chapter 3.

coach_feedback.scaffold_hint: Think about what the OT will need weeks from now to prove the client actually improved — which of these options gives you something comparable over time? Take another look at the case with that in mind, and pick again.
coach_feedback.feedback: You explained why standardized tools matter in your own words, which shows real comprehension rather than just recalling the term "standardized."
coach_feedback.next_step: How would you apply that reasoning to choose between two standardized assessments for a specific client — what would make one a better fit than the other?
coach_feedback.textbook_pointer: Review assessment selection criteria in Chapter 5.

coach_feedback.scaffold_hint: The client has a fixed discharge date coming up fast. Which of these options is the one thing that has to happen BEFORE that date to catch problems while there's still time to fix them? Take another look at the case with that in mind, and pick again.
coach_feedback.feedback: You correctly weighed what actually needs to happen before this specific discharge date, rather than defaulting to a general safety habit.
coach_feedback.next_step: How would you change this plan if the client lived alone with no caregiver support at all — what would you prioritize differently?
coach_feedback.textbook_pointer: Review discharge planning guidance in Chapter 2.

coach_feedback.scaffold_hint: Look at the two pieces of information in the case separately — one came directly from the client's own words, the other from something the OT measured. Which one is Subjective? Take another look at the case with that in mind, and pick again.
coach_feedback.feedback: You correctly separated what the client said from what was measured. The next step is applying that distinction to a real note, not just naming it.
coach_feedback.next_step: Given this same client, which detail goes in Objective, and how would that combination shape your Assessment?
coach_feedback.textbook_pointer: Review SOAP note structure in Chapter 4.

coach_feedback.scaffold_hint: Think about which option keeps the client actively doing the task themselves, versus which ones remove the challenge or delay it entirely. Take another look at the case with that in mind, and pick again.
coach_feedback.feedback: You picked the approach that builds independence directly rather than the ones that remove the challenge or delay it.
coach_feedback.trap: choosing an assessment when the stage calls for intervention (or vice versa)
coach_feedback.next_step: If this client plateaus at this level of dressing independence after several sessions, how would you decide whether to keep grading the same task or introduce adaptive equipment sooner than usual?
coach_feedback.textbook_pointer: Review hemiparesis retraining techniques in Chapter 6.

scaffold_fallback: Take another look at the case stem — which detail did you weigh most heavily when you chose your answer, and is there another detail in the case that matters just as much? Reconsider with that in mind, and pick again.

explanations.text:
Before I explain, tell me this: when you picture a wrist splint, are you thinking about what it holds still, or about what it's letting move?

A splint's job is defined as much by what it blocks as by what it allows. A resting hand splint, for example, positions the wrist and fingers to prevent contracture, while a dynamic splint uses tension to actively assist a weak movement, like extending a finger after a tendon repair. The choice between them depends on the goal: protecting a healing structure calls for a static design, while regaining active movement calls for a dynamic one.

Think of it like a cast versus a resistance band — a cast (static splint) holds a position, a resistance band (dynamic splint) actively works a motion. Mixing the two up is a common early mistake: prescribing a static splint when the client actually needs graded, active resistance.

Now you try: a client six weeks post flexor tendon repair is ready to start light active motion. Would a static or dynamic splint fit that stage of healing, and why?

For the full classification system and trim-line diagrams, read the orthotics section of Chapter 3 in your TherapyEd book.

First — when you say sensory processing is confusing, is it the different sensory systems that are unclear, or how a child's reaction connects to a specific system?

Sensory processing describes how the nervous system receives and organizes information from the senses, then produces a response. A child who covers their ears at a normal-volume classroom might be over-responsive to auditory input — the sensation registers as more intense than it actually is. A child who doesn't notice a shirt tag or a scraped knee might be under-responsive, needing more input before a sensation registers at all.

A useful comparison: over-responsivity is like a smoke detector that's too sensitive, going off from steam. Under-responsivity is a smoke detector with a weak battery, not going off even when there's real smoke — same system, opposite sensitivity.

Now apply it: if a child seeks out spinning and jumping constantly throughout the day, which pattern does that most likely reflect, and what would you want to observe next to confirm it?

For the full breakdown of sensory systems and response patterns, review the sensory integration section of Chapter 7 in your TherapyEd book.

Quick check first: is it the concept of "therapeutic use of self" that feels vague, or knowing when to use it differently with different clients?

Therapeutic use of self means intentionally using your own personality, communication style, and interpersonal approach as part of the intervention — not just as bedside manner. With an anxious client, that might mean a calm, predictable pace and clear explanations before each step. With a discouraged client, it might mean naming small wins explicitly instead of assuming they'll notice their own progress.

Think of it like adjusting your teaching style for different students: the content doesn't change, but how you deliver it does, based on what that person needs to actually receive it.

Now think it through: a client keeps deflecting with humor whenever a session gets emotionally difficult. How would you adjust your therapeutic use of self to keep the session productive without shutting down their coping style?

For structured models of therapeutic use of self, read the professional communication section of Chapter 8 in your TherapyEd book.

Before I explain — when you break down an activity, are you getting stuck on which components to look for, or on how to connect them back to a client's specific deficit?

Activity analysis means breaking a task into its physical, cognitive, and social-emotional demands, then comparing those demands to a client's abilities. Making a cup of coffee, for example, demands standing balance, bilateral coordination, sequencing, and safety awareness around heat — all at once. Naming each demand separately is what lets you decide which part of the task to grade up or down.

A helpful comparison: it's similar to reading a recipe's ingredient list before cooking — you can't adjust the dish well if you don't know what's actually in it.

Now apply it: for a client with impaired sequencing after a brain injury, which single demand of the coffee-making task would you grade down first, and what would that adaptation look like?

For a full activity analysis worksheet and examples, review Chapter 2 of your TherapyEd book.

First — is SOAP note structure itself unclear, or is it deciding which details go in which section?

SOAP stands for Subjective, Objective, Assessment, and Plan. Subjective is what the client reports in their own words. Objective is what you measure or directly observe — range of motion, test scores, time on task. Assessment is your clinical interpretation of what the subjective and objective data mean together. Plan is what happens next.

A simple way to keep them straight: Subjective is what they say, Objective is what you see or measure, Assessment is what you think it means, Plan is what you'll do about it.

Now try it: a client says their hand "feels weak today," and you measure their grip strength at 5 lbs below baseline. Which detail is Subjective, which is Objective, and how would that combination shape your Assessment?

For full SOAP note examples, review the documentation section of Chapter 4 in your TherapyEd book.

Quick question first: is discharge planning unclear as a concept, or is it deciding what to prioritize when time is limited?

Discharge planning means preparing a client — and often their caregivers — for the transition out of your care, so gains made in therapy actually carry over into daily life. That includes home safety changes, caregiver training, and making sure the client or family knows the warning signs that would mean they need to seek help again.

Think of it like packing for a trip: you're not just packing what's useful in the session room, you're packing for the environment the client is actually going home to.

Now apply it: if a client's caregiver is present for only one visit before discharge, what would you prioritize teaching them in that single session?

For discharge planning checklists, review Chapter 2 of your TherapyEd book.

explain_fallback: Happy to walk through something with you — which concept would you like explained? For example, you could name a topic like splinting, sensory processing, therapeutic use of self, activity analysis, SOAP note documentation, or discharge planning, and I'll dig into it with you.
progress_notes: You're building a solid practice history across a mix of domains, and your recent attempts show steady follow-through on the reasoning prompts, not just picking an answer. Keep pushing on the domains where accuracy is lower — that's where a little focused review pays off fastest. Rereading the chapter sections tied to your most recent misses is a good next step before your next practice set.

Your practice pattern shows real engagement with the reasoning prompts, which mirrors the real exam well. Where you're strongest, a quick review is enough. Where accuracy dips, slow down and re-explain your reasoning out loud before you check the answer key.

You're still early in building a full picture of your strengths, but the pattern so far suggests your reasoning is more consistent than your first-attempt accuracy — a sign that talking through the "why," and working through the hints when you get one, is helping. Keep practicing at this pace, and revisit the textbook sections tied to any domain where you've seen more than one miss.
